newsitem.title: INDONESIA: SE Asian Grain - Prices in doldrums on ample stocks.
newsitem.headline: SE Asian Grain - Prices in doldrums on ample stocks.

text.p: Southeast Asian grains and oilseeds prices are expected to remain in the doldrums this week due to more than ample supplies and high stocks in a dull pre-Christmas market, regional traders said on Wednesday.
"Business was really good at the end of last year due to tight supply following a drought. But it has been slow this year," a trader in Indonesia said.
"A couple of feedmills were looking into buying soymeal last week, but there's been no news of anyone making a commitment yet," said a trader with a flour and feed mill in Kuala Lumpur.
Singapore-based traders said last week that Malaysian importers were in the market for soymeal but local dealers in Kuala Lumpur could not confirm this.
"People are also looking for maize from China but I don't think this is going to be done before the beginning of next year," said another trader in the Malaysian capital.
Indonesian grain prices were flat, traders said.
Corn was quoted at 375-380 rupiaha kg in Jakarta, unchanged from a week ago, although trades were mostly at the lower end of the range, dealers said. Soymeal was unchanged at 795-800 rupiah.
The traders said the harvest in the key producing region of Lampung in South Sumatra was proceeding, with arrivals expected to peak in January.
"There has been some rain but nothing bad enough to affect the harvest," one Lampung trader said. "Buying interest has been thin because buyers seem to be well stocked."
A Jakarta-based trader said soymeal imports were continuing to arrive, but no new business was heard in the market.
Data from Belawan Port showed that 11,700 tonnes of Indian origin soymeal was scheduled to arrive at the North Sumatran port on December 25.
In Malaysia, traders said domestic corn prices took another dip while wheat and soymeal held steady despite thin demand.
The price of bulk corn, ex-factory/godown in Malaysia's central region was quoted at between 425-430 ringgit a tonne against 445-460 ringgit in the previous week.
"A" grade wheat in bags, ex-factory/godown in the central region was unchanged at 800 ringgit a tonne. The price of low-grade wheat, also central-based, was steady at 450 ringgit.
Soymeal was at 820 ringgit for local material and 810 for imported soymeal, both in the central region.

Oil crushers in Thailand recently bought 50,000 tonnes of U.S. soybeans, but there was little else in the way of business as rising supplies of soymeal and corn kept buying interest at bay, traders said.
"We have enough to cover January-February. Any buying now will not be for nearby shipment," said one feedmill manager.
The Thai Cottonseed, Ricebran and Vegetable Oil Crushers Association bought the 50,000 tonnes of soybeans for February shipment. The price was said to be slightly below US$300 a tonne C&F Bangkok.

Ample supplies of soymeal and corn dragged local prices down, the traders said. Soymeal prices were quoted around 9.00 baht a kg from 9.00-9.30 baht last week. Corn prices eased to 4.05-4.16 baht a kg from 4.10-4.20 baht a kg last week.
Aside from the 50,000 tonnes of soybeans purchased by the crushers, more than 60,000 tonnes of imported soymeal should arrive between now and the end of January, 1997.
At least 40,000 tonnes of U.S. and Argentine soymeal and 12,650 tonnes of Argentine sunflower meal entered the market last week, traders said.

"I guess many would like to assess their demand after February when major festivities end before buying. Moreover, local soybean output will start entering the market from late March. They have to take this into account," a trader said.
"However, if the prices are attractive, buying interest will emerge again," he added.
Besides soybeans and soymeal, about 30,000 tonnes of wheat arrived at Thai ports this month.
Industry sources said the domestic demand outlook for wheat remains robust due to strong demand from the food industry.
But demand for feed wheat will continue to be pressured by the depressed shrimp industry which is an important consumer of feed wheat.
Thailand imported 665,501 tonnes of wheat in 1995 compared with 671,452 tonnes in 1994 and 572,198 tonnes in 1993.
